haṁsa
(‘that which moves gracefully’)
------------------------------------------
‘Haṁsa’ is one of the words in Sanskrit that has been used in several senses such as: the swan, the sun, a king who has transcended worldly desires, विष्णु, शिव, परमात्मन् (the Supreme Self), the jīvātman (individual सोउल्), a particular type of horse and so on.
However, the bird swan is the most widely accepted meaning.
There was a widespread belief in the ancient days that the bird swan had the special power to separate milk from water and drink it, leaving the water behind (vide Śukla Yajurveda 19.73). This gave rise to the maxim Haṁsa-kṣīra-nyāya. It means the capacity to separate the good from the bad, accept only the good and reject the bad.
Saṁnyāsins (ascetics or मोन्क्स्) have been divided into four orders, of which the ‘haṁsas’ are the third. They stay not more than one night in a village, reside outside it in the night, entering it only for alms and carry one दण्ड or staff.
Tha मन्त्र (mystical formula) “so’ham haṁsaḥ” (‘He is myself and I am He’) is called ‘haṁsamantra’ and is specially used by the saṁnyāsins of the advaita school of philosophy for constant जप or repetition.
Haṁsa was one of the generals of the Magadhan emperor जरासन्ध mentioned in the Mahābhārata (Sabhāparva, 13).

Haṁsagītā
(‘the Song of the Swan’)
------------------------------------------
As the Bhagavadgītā of the Mahā-bhārata became extremely popular, many more Gītās, in imitation of it, were composed by later writers. They were either integrated into the पुराणस् or were circulated as independent works. Out of the 36 such Gītās, the Haṁsagītā is also one. It forms a part of the Bhāgavata (11.13.16-42).
When the four sages led by सनक questioned their ड़थेर्, ब्रह्मा, about the way of freeing oneself from the clutches of the guṇas, he remembered his ड़थेर् (Mahāviṣṇu or नारायण), since he himself did not know the answer. Then Mahāviṣṇu appeared there in the form of a हṁस or swan and taught them the way. This has been christened as Haṁsagītā.
A brief summary of this गीता is as follows:
The आत्मन् is one only and not many. The प्रकृति, out of which the various bodies have been made, is also one only. The मिन्द् of the जीव gets attached to viṣayas or objects of senses and this creates सṁस्कारस् (strong tendencies) in it. By meditating upon one’s Self as परमात्मन् (Supreme Self) and also by an analysis of three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् (jāgrat, स्वप्न and सुषुप्ति or waking, dream and deep-sleep states) that leads to the conviction that one is the spirit beyond these three states, one can transcend this attachment to the guṇas (sattva, रजस् and तमस्). The three fold discipline viz., śravaṇa (hearing about the आत्मन्), मनन (reflecting on it) and निदिध्यासन (meditating on it) will help in achieving this. Once a person realises himself as the आत्मन्, he becomes freed from all bondages though he has to live for some more time due to prārabdha or residual कर्म. However, this will never affect his मिन्द्.
There is a Haṁsagītā in the Mahā-bhārata (Śāntiparva 299) also. It teaches the necessity of developing the virtues like truthfulness, self-control, forbearance and forgiveness in order to realise the ultimate Reality.

Haṁsopaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a minor Upaniṣad assigned to the Śukla Yajurveda. It has just 21 mantras, both in prose and in poetry (as ślokas in the anuṣṭubh meter).
It begins with a question by the sage गौतम to the venerable Sanatkumāra, reputed to be a mānasaputra or mindborn son, of the four faced ब्रह्मा. The question is: ‘By what means can one get the knowledge of (the Supreme) ब्रह्मन्?’
Sanatkumāra replies that he got this knowledge from पार्वती, the divine spouse of Lord शिव and that it should be kept always a secret. However, it can be taught to worthy disciples.
Brahman is pervading everything even as fire pervades fuel or oil pervades oil seeds. Having known it, one transcends death.
Then the method of raising the prāṇavāyu or the vital air from the मूलाधार (the lowest of the six चक्रस्) right up to the सहस्रार near the ब्रह्मरन्ध्र, is described. There, the योगि beholds परमात्मन् (the Supreme Self), resplendent as millions of suns.
Entering of the jīvātman (the indi-vidual सोउल्) into the various petals of the ‘heart-lotus’ (hṛtpadma) and the consequent results, are delineated next.
This is followed by instructions regarding the जप of the ajapā-हṁस-मन्त्र (“so’haṁ haṁsaḥ”) with the concomitants. (See जप">AJAPĀJAPA.) The जप is to be done with every breath, the total number of breathings per day of 24 hours being 21,600.
This जप leads to the mystical experience of various kinds of sounds like those of a bell, a conch, a lute and cymbals. Their results are described in the next section.
The Upaniṣad ends with the final result of the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्, viz., dissolution of the मिन्द् and shining in the glory of that ब्रह्मन्.
